title: Dispatch brief contract
desc: A compact dispatch contract requiring required house skill reads, a concrete goal, files, approach, constraints, code sample, verification, ownership, and exit criteria so delegated work can execute and return a self-test artifact.
steps: OWNER RULE 2026-09-29, FIRST MOVE WHEN A SECTOR WANDERS: re-brief with SHARP SAMPLE CODE for BOTH the extraction module proto and the wiring proto -- the whole new function as runnable code, the exact lines to insert at the seam with their anchor line, and the rule that every other byte of the wired copy stays identical (deletions 0, no proto name inside it). Measured the same day: a message-system sector given only copy canonical plus the seam returned 13 deleted comment lines and a proto-named dot-source; the same sector given the full replacement code returned a 2 plus 0 diff in one round, and a queue reader was fixed in one round once the atomic-rename code was pasted. Prose descriptions make a cheap tier design; code makes it apply. DECISION: five CONTENT rules ride inside the ten parts, and each exists because a real dispatch failed without it. WHEN: you have the ten-part skeleton and are filling it in. HOW: run wkappbot skill read harness-agent-brief-guard for what the harness enforces and wkappbot skill read verify-tool-or-guard-synthetic-live-static for what counts as proof, then check your draft against these five before sending. WHAT A SECTOR CAN ACTUALLY BE ASKED FOR, the owner's question 2026-09-12, asked because it was not written down anywhere in one place. THE THREE ARTIFACTS are the deliverable: a MODULE PROTO extracting the logic into its own file, a WIRED PROTO that is a byte copy of canonical carrying only the seam so the diff is readable, and an ARGLESS SELF TEST with an inversion control. THE EVIDENCE YOU MAY DEMAND, and the common property is that a sector cannot author it: a FILE LISTING, asked for BEFORE any number, since a tally is typeable and a directory listing is not; a git diff numstat; AND FOR A READ-ONLY MEASUREMENT SECTOR, AN EVIDENCE FILE AT A PATH ROOT NAMES, which is both the artifact ROOT wants and the structural trace that stops the debrief gate charging the NEXT dispatch for a round that actually succeeded with insertions minus deletions stated; an IMPORT check in a fresh interpreter, never a parse check, because a parse cannot resolve a name; the RAW output of a run, first line to last, tracebacks included; the INVERSION actually executed, the fixed line removed and the suite shown red and then restored; and a COUNT the page or program computed rather than a word. WHAT YOU MAY NOT ASK FOR, each costing a whole round when it appears in a brief: a direct edit to canonical, since write-freeze returns a proto instead; a python RUN, since the cheap tier is interpreter-frozen in this repo and answers a question about output by READING the source and reporting it as verification; an adjective such as confirm or verify, which one word satisfies; and more than one judgement per brief, since nine classifications came back as a report that corrected its own tally twice and added to eight. AND A .txt UNDER .tmp IS NOT A DELIVERABLE -- it reads as finished to the sector and as absent to everyone else, which cost a full round the same day. ABSORBED RULE FOLLOWS: FIRST, NAME THE TOOL, not just the action -- cp for a whole-file promotion, the Edit tool for an in-place change, wkappbot file write with a source file when the dispatched model is write-frozen on canonical source. A brief saying edit this file leaves the method open, and an agent that hits a frozen tool stops with the work half done. SECOND, KILL THE INVENTED BLOCKER BEFORE IT IS INVENTED: if the task depends on a capability existing, name the FILE and LINE proving it. A sector claimed a broker amend API did not exist and shipped weaker behaviour instead; the API was one field VALUE away from the cancel call in the same function, and the repo said so in writing. THIRD, TELL IT A RED TEST IS A FINDING -- state that production logic must not be changed to make a test pass, and that a test still failing after the fixture is correct must STOP the work and be reported as the most valuable outcome available. That sentence is what turned a failing test into the discovery that the KR sell re-price was wired to a function which deliberately refuses sells. FOURTH, SILENCE IS A DEFECT: in trading code a dropped record, a branch that prints nothing, or a swallowed rejection is a bug and never a design choice -- say so, or an agent will write a test asserting that malformed holdings VANISH and call it a pass. FIFTH, FORBID FLATTERING NUMBERS: say plainly that a corrected measurement showing a WORSE result is the right outcome. WHY: all five were paid for in wasted rounds on 2026-08-07, and each is far cheaper as one sentence in the brief than as a re-dispatch. //why:gate refusal is a task requiring routing judgment-haiku //why:Mandatory on-load and three-tier skill requirement for sector dispatch-sonnet //why:Brief content includes executable code samples, not prose descriptions-haiku

NAVIGATION AND VERIFICATION COMMANDS. Related: wkappbot skill read proto-to-live-wiring-howto (the promotion sequence these briefs feed); wkappbot skill read verify-tool-or-guard-synthetic-live-static-howto (a guard is verified by what it REFUSES, run it never read it); wkappbot skill read delegation-verify-scorecard (the diff-verify rubric); wkappbot skill read harness-agent-brief-guard (what blocks a dispatch and how to satisfy it); wkappbot skill read opus-self-reflection (verify the artifact, not the report). THE THREE COMMANDS THAT CAUGHT EVERY REAL DEFECT IN THE 2026-09-04 SESSION, run them yourself on the delegate's artifact before accepting it: 'diff <canonical> <candidate>' must be non-empty and confined to the seam; 'wc -l <candidate>' must respect the cap without deletions elsewhere; and one per-invariant loop -- for t in TOKEN1 TOKEN2 TOKEN3; do echo $t canonical=$(grep -c $t <canonical>) candidate=$(grep -c $t <candidate>); done -- counted SEPARATELY, because a combined grep totalled 6 against 6 while every component had changed. //why:ROOT verifies artifact by comparing against canonical, not by reading sector report //why:structural checks catch defects a tally cannot see //why:diff canonical vs candidate, wc-l, and per-invariant count are the verification commands-sonnet //why:diff canonical vs candidate, wc-l, and per-invariant count are the verification commands-sonnet //why:structural checks catch defects a tally cannot see-haiku

DECISION: a brief that changes a function SIGNATURE must require BOTH DOORS OPEN -- old and new callable at once, one delegating to the other -- as the emergency step, with the proper cleanup done slowly afterwards. Owner's standing rule, 2026-08-07. WHEN: any brief that adds, removes or reorders a parameter on a function something else already calls. HOW: instruct the agent to keep the existing call shape working unchanged, add the new shape beside it, and have one delegate to the other so there is exactly one implementation; then say plainly in the brief that removing the old door is a LATER, separate task. WHY: measured the same day and the owner had to point it out. I added a fifth parameter to decide_anchor_update as a REQUIRED positional. Origin still held a four-argument caller, so a module, its host, a sell-reprice module and a balance normalizer all became one indivisible push -- and promoting the module alone killed the canonical host outright with TypeError missing 1 required positional argument. Every round after that spent effort managing a coupling that never needed to exist. THE DEFAULT MUST BE CHOSEN WITH CARE, which is the part a brief has to spell out: defaulting the new parameter to a plain value is NOT automatically compatible. Here, defaulting anchor_exists to False would have let a fallback top-up SET the anchor under the new rule, reviving the exact starvation the change existed to cure. The honest default is a sentinel meaning THE CALLER DID NOT SAY, whose branch reproduces the OLD behaviour faithfully. A default that changes behaviour for existing callers is a breaking change wearing a compatible signature. THE TEST THAT PROVES IT is not the module's own suite -- every one of its cases passes the new argument explicitly -- but running the UNCHANGED caller and watching it complete. //why:dispatch shape: keep old callable alongside new to avoid breaking callers //why:old and new callable at once, one delegating to the other, prevents breaking callers on promotion-sonnet //why:used this pattern when writing gg-main.ps1 function helpers that must stay callable while being extended-sonnet //why:dispatch shape: keep old callable alongside new to avoid breaking callers-sonnet

NEVER put a NUMERIC UNICODE ESCAPE in a brief when the target file must stay pure ASCII -- name the unicode BLOCK instead. WHEN: the code you are specifying needs a non-ASCII character range (a Hangul range, a CJK range, an emoji range) inside a file a pre-commit hook requires to be pure ASCII. HOW: write the pattern with a named block, for example the .NET form backslash-p-brace-IsHangulSyllables-brace, and add one line saying the block name must NOT be substituted with the characters it denotes; run wkappbot skill read harness-edit-write-skill-bypass for the pure-ASCII commit rule this protects. WHY: measured 2026-09-03 in wkappbot-kih on an agy transcript reader. The brief specified a character class using the backslash-u form for the two ends of the Hangul syllables block. The delegate RESOLVED the escapes and wrote the two Korean characters literally into the .ps1; the bytes then mangled, the live pattern became an unterminated character class, and every call threw ArgumentException while the function still returned records with empty text -- a throw inside a loop that leaves a plausible-looking result. THE PART THAT MAKES THIS A BRIEF RULE AND NOT A DELEGATE RULE: writing the corrected brief, I emitted the same substitution TWICE myself, and the Edit tool reported old and new identical because both sides had become the same Korean text. An author who cannot reliably type the escape cannot reliably review it either. A block NAME is ASCII in every hop -- author, brief file, delegate, source file, hook -- and there is nothing in it for anyone to helpfully resolve. THE GENERAL FORM: prefer a notation that has no correct expansion over one whose expansion is what you are trying to prevent. //why:Used block names instead of unicode literals in Hangul pattern briefs this session //why:Use named blocks for unicode ranges in ASCII-target files. //why:kept all bash source fixes this session pure ASCII, matching this documented constraint-haiku //why:Use named blocks for unicode ranges in ASCII-target files.-haiku

VERIFIED: TWO CHEAP READS CATCH A NO-OP SEAM AND AN IMPOSSIBLE SUITE, both without running anything. WHEN: a sector returns a pure predicate plus its seam, and the report says done. HOW: run wkappbot skill read verify-tool-or-guard-synthetic-live-static-howto for the run-it discipline this precedes, then do two things before any build. FIRST, grep the CALL SITES and read the arguments: any parameter passed as the same literal at every site is not an input, it is a decision written in the wrong place, and if that literal makes the predicate constant the feature is a no-op. SECOND, scan the self-test for two cases sharing IDENTICAL arguments with OPPOSITE expectations -- that is a contradiction no implementation can satisfy, so the suite cannot have been run. WHY: measured 2026-09-05 on a hint-suppression predicate, and the two defects were the same round. The module was genuinely good -- pure, four real comparisons, exits non-zero on failure -- but all three seams passed bytes-written as 0 and pace-over as false, so the predicate could only ever return true and the hints printed exactly as often as before. THAT IS THE MIRROR OF THE ROUND BEFORE IT, which suppressed always; both looked correct at the seam, and the name on the function said budget in each case. Meanwhile its cases 2 and 3 called with the same four arguments and expected opposite answers, and the arithmetic settles which loses: 29500 plus 500 is exactly 30000, the comparison is strictly greater, so the predicate returns true and case 2 must fail. THE RULE WORTH KEEPING: a constant argument and a self-contradicting suite are both visible in the SOURCE, so they cost one read each -- spend that before you spend a build, and treat a done report over an impossible suite as proof the suite was never executed. //why:Verified cheap reads catch no-op seams //why:two cheap reads catch no-op seams and impossible suites before dispatch //why:the resting-order bypass at host 687 is a decision inlined into a filter where no test can reach it-opus //why:the resting-order bypass at host 687 is a decision inlined into a filter where no test can reach it-opus //why:two cheap reads catch no-op seams and impossible suites before dispatch-sonnet

RESULT: the SEARCH-not-NAME rule and Agent.cmd's own brief-guard CONTRADICT each other, and the way through is three CONFIRMED-HEALTHY named reads plus searches for the rest. WHEN: you apply the owner rule about not naming crowded skills and the dispatch is then refused for missing skill references. HOW: run wkappbot skill read agent-brief-standard-template for the ten-part shape, note the score line that every wkappbot skill edit prints, and name only skills whose score you have SEEN at or above the floor this session -- then give search terms for everything else. WHY: measured 2026-09-06. Agent.cmd's brief-guard counts literal wkappbot skill read occurrences and refuses a brief that carries only searches, while the fleet tier gate refuses a brief that NAMES a skill scoring under 60. Satisfying one alone fails the other; naming three known-healthy skills satisfies both. Also measured the same hour: Agent.cmd takes its prompt as a quoted argument or via --file, and a plain stdin redirect yields No prompt provided -- the --file form is the one that carries a long multiline brief intact. //why:assemble the whole brief shape once before dispatching a root //why:Every sector this session went through first time once the brief carried both mandatory reads plus three healthy task skills -- the refusals I paid were all for omissions in my first draft, never for the task.-opus //why:It happened again 2026-09-19, four refusals in a row naming four DIFFERENT omissions -- a -ref tier as reading, no model field, the five labels, then the three artifacts plus a FENCED sample. One contract-complete draft, never incremental appeasement.-opus //why:assemble the whole brief shape once before dispatching a root-sonnet

RESULT: the do-not-name-a-flag-in-your-brief rule was a rule about a BUG, and the bug is now fixed. WHEN: writing a delegation brief that needs to mention a command-line flag in its prose, or reading an older note telling you that you cannot. HOW: name the flag normally -- wkappbot skill read codex-tool-wrappers for the dispatcher contract -- and keep the companion-file habit only for MULTI-LINE sample code, where it earns its place because a brief is prose and code pasted into prose gets reflowed. WHY: measured 2026-09-06. The wkclaude argument splitter classified ANY hyphen-led token as a claude option wherever it appeared, so a brief whose prose merely named a flag had that word lifted out of the prompt and forwarded to claude.exe, which died with unknown option; all three dispatch routes failed identically because they converge on one loop. The fix is a seen-prompt flag: once prompt text has begun, every later token is prompt, hyphen or not. TWO ROUNDS DIED ON THIS BEFORE ANYONE LOOKED AT THE SPLITTER, and the workaround got written down as if it were a design rule -- which is how a defect becomes doctrine. When a tool refuses a shape that ought to work, fix the tool before you teach the workaround. //why:Brief standard template rule //why:brief template rule //why:Sector delivers code samples in .tmp, ROOT promotes to canonical

RESULT: the experiment settled step 5 and the answer is WORSE than a quote bug -- brief CONTENT becomes COMMAND-LINE ARGUMENTS, so any hyphen-led token inside a brief is parsed as a CLI option. WHEN: writing any brief that must mention a flag, a PowerShell parameter, or a command line -- which is most briefs about tooling. HOW: run wkappbot skill read codex-tool-wrappers for the dispatcher family, then write flags WITHOUT their leading hyphens and say so in words -- the LiteralPath parameter, the file parameter, the nth flag -- and keep the no-double-quote rule as well; verify before dispatch with two greps over the brief, one counting the double-quote character and one counting occurrences of a space followed by a hyphen, and require both to be zero. WHY: measured 2026-09-05 by a deliberate probe. A --file brief was sent whose body explained, in prose, that the dispatcher reads content with Get-Content and a certain PowerShell path parameter. The dispatch died with claude.exe error unknown option and the parameter name from MY OWN BRIEF TEXT quoted back as the offending option, exit 1. So the content does not merely survive Get-Content and stop there: Agent.ps1 reads it whole and then passes it onward as an ARGUMENT, where the downstream CLI tokenizes it again. THIS CONFIRMS step 4 and CORRECTS the source reading in step 5 -- the Get-Content -Raw call is real and is not the whole path, and a diagnosis that stops at the read is half a diagnosis. THE SHAPE WORTH KEEPING: a failed experiment that names the offending token is worth more than a passing one, because the error message quoted the exact byte of my own brief that did the damage. //why:Before dispatch grep the brief for the double-quote char and for space-then-hyphen and require both zero-opus //why:Explains several brief-quote-gate false positives I hit this session dispatching investigation sectors -- avoiding hyphen-led tokens and repeated skill-name mentions in brief bodies going forward.-sonnet //why:Explains several brief-quote-gate false positives I hit this session dispatching investigation sectors -- avoiding hyphen-led tokens and repeated skill-name mentions in brief bodies going forward.-sonnet
